JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- The atmosphere was tense in Cape Town on Friday after xenophobic violence that has left more than 40 dead in Johannesburg spread to South Africa's largest city. Immigrants from Mozambique line up in Primrose, South Africa, to board buses back home. Clashes overnight resulted in one death and 15 arrests and the evacuations of 420 foreign nationals, a police official in Cape Town said. "Crowds of people went on a rampage, looting and carrying out acts of violence," said Cape Town Police Superintendent Billy Jones. They were charged with public violence and are to appear in court Monday. One foreign national, a Somali, died when he was run over by a vehicle as he tried to escape the angry crowds, Jones said. Twelve people suffered minor injuries. He said Friday was tense but calm, with state and local police stationed throughout the area. Jack Bloom of the opposition party Democratic Alliance told CNN on Friday that government troops were helping police ward off violence in Johannesburg. Aid workers and volunteers were providing tents, food and supplies at the police stations. Bloom estimated that about 2,000 foreigners had sought haven at those locations. It was the first violence in the coastal city since a wave of xenophobia began about two weeks ago in Johannesburg, resulting in at least 42 deaths. The foreign nationals were transported from the city after angry crowds formed at a public meeting seeking to calm tensions, Jones told CNN. They were being housed at community centers and churches. The attacks in South Africa have forced thousands of immigrants to flee, prompting neighboring Mozambique to declare a state of emergency on Friday. Desperate stories of those fleeing violence . The country's Foreign Minister Oldemiro Baloi said the decision was taken after about 10,000 Mozambicans fled from South Africa. CNN's Robyn Curnow reported long lines of people -- including many from Zimbabwe and Mozambique -- waiting for buses in Johannesburg to take them home. Bloom, from Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg, said the attacks on foreigners who fled to South Africa for a better life has become a "humanitarian crisis." South African President Thabo Mbeki has approved the deployment of the army to help stop the attacks, which have drawn condemnation from South African officials and other African leaders. About 28,000 people have been displaced by the violence, Hangwani Malaudzi, a spokesman for the Ministry of Safety and Security said. And more than 400 have been arrested for crimes ranging from murder, to causing a public disturbance, he said. The country has also seen a disturbing throwback to the 1980s apartheid-era lynching tactic of "necklacing," which was widely used in the townships at the time. Used on suspected informants, the "necklace" is a car tire, filled with petrol, put around the person's neck and set alight. The victims are mainly immigrants and refugees from other parts of Africa, including Zimbabwe, where a devastated economy has sent at least two million people across the border in search of a better life. Some say the attacks stem from a long-standing feeling among locals that the number of immigrants in South Africa results in shortages of jobs and essential needs. Inadequate housing, a lack of running water and electricity, the rising prices of food, and escalating crime -- nearly 20,000 people were slain in South Africa last year -- add to the resentment.  Watch analysis of reasons behind xenophobic attacks » . According to South Africa's latest census, the country has about 45 million people. The South African Department of Human Affairs estimates that more than 4 million people reside in South Africa illegally, but that figure is based on a 10-year-old study and some feel the number of immigrants in South Africa is much higher. Some say that millions have recently fled to South Africa from Zimbabwe because of violence there since the county's stalled election. A presidential run-off between long-time leader President Robert Mugabe and his opposition challenger, Morgan Tsvangirai, is scheduled for June 27 in Zimbabwe -- three months after the initial vote. Zimbabwe also is in the midst of an economic collapse, with nearly 80 percent unemployment.

Aid organizations warned that the sudden movement of people was placing additional pressure on neighboring states already struggling with poverty and, in Zimbabwe’s case, political and economic turmoil. South Africa deployed military personnel to support police—the first such domestic deployment since the end of apartheid—as officials sought to contain the unrest. Government leaders condemned the attacks and said foreign nationals had a right to protection.

## South Africa’s 2008 Xenophobic Violence Exposed Deep Social and Regional Crises

**JOHANNESBURG —** In May 2008, a wave of xenophobic violence swept through South African townships and informal settlements, killing more than 60 people, injuring hundreds and forcing tens of thousands of foreign nationals from their homes.

The attacks began on May 11 in Alexandra, a densely populated township north of Johannesburg, before spreading across Gauteng province and into Cape Town, Durban and other parts of the country. Mobs targeted immigrants—particularly Zimbabweans, Mozambicans, Malawians and Somalis—accusing them of taking jobs, housing and business opportunities from South Africans.

By the time the violence subsided, commonly cited official figures put the death toll at **62**, including more than 20 South Africans mistaken for foreigners or caught in the unrest. About **670 people were injured**, and police made roughly **1,300 to 1,400 arrests** for offenses including murder, assault, robbery and public violence. Exact totals varied among government agencies and humanitarian organizations.

### Poverty and Competition Fueled Attacks

The violence emerged from a volatile mix of unemployment, poverty, inadequate housing and poor public services. Nearly 14 years after the end of apartheid, many Black South Africans remained confined to impoverished communities with limited economic opportunities.

Foreign nationals became convenient scapegoats for broader failures in housing, service delivery and employment. Rumors that immigrants accepted lower wages, obtained state housing fraudulently or were responsible for crime intensified resentment. Small shops run by Somali and other African migrants were looted and burned.

Researchers and human-rights organizations also pointed to weak policing, inflammatory local leadership, corruption in immigration enforcement and a long-standing culture of hostility toward African migrants. Although widely described as “xenophobic,” the attacks primarily targeted Black Africans from elsewhere on the continent rather than all foreigners.

### Tens of Thousands Driven From Their Homes

The unrest displaced **tens of thousands of people**. Estimates differed, but humanitarian groups said as many as **100,000 foreign nationals were uprooted nationwide**, while many thousands left South Africa altogether. Mozambicans, Zimbabweans and others crowded into police stations, churches, community halls and temporary camps.

Several thousand Mozambicans were repatriated, while many Zimbabweans crossed back into their country despite the severe political and economic crisis there. Temporary displacement camps around Johannesburg and Cape Town later became controversial because of overcrowding, cold weather, inadequate sanitation and government pressure on residents to reintegrate into communities where they feared renewed attacks.

### “Necklacing” Revived Memories of Apartheid-Era Violence

One of the crisis’s most shocking features was the use of **“necklacing,”** in which a tire is placed around a victim’s neck or body, soaked with fuel and set alight. The method had become notorious during the violent final years of apartheid, when it was sometimes used against suspected police informers and political opponents.

The best-known victim in 2008 was **Ernesto Alfabeto Nhamuave**, a Mozambican man who was beaten and burned alive in the Ramaphosa informal settlement east of Johannesburg. Photographs of his death became an enduring symbol of the attacks and provoked national and international outrage.

### Zimbabwe’s Collapse Increased Migration

The violence occurred as neighboring Zimbabwe faced political repression and economic collapse. President **Robert Mugabe**, in power since independence in 1980, was fighting to retain control after opposition leader **Morgan Tsvangirai** won more votes in the March 2008 presidential election but, according to official results, not enough to avoid a runoff.

The period before the June runoff was marked by widespread intimidation, beatings and killings of opposition supporters. Tsvangirai withdrew, saying the violence made a credible election impossible, leaving Mugabe to run alone.

Zimbabwe’s economy was also unraveling. Hyperinflation destroyed wages and savings, shops lacked basic goods, public services deteriorated, and unemployment was often estimated at **80 percent or higher**, although reliable measurements were difficult. Crop failures, controversial land reforms, declining industrial production and government mismanagement contributed to the collapse. Western sanctions targeted Mugabe and senior officials, but the government blamed them more broadly for the country’s economic distress.

Millions of Zimbabweans left the country, with South Africa their principal destination. Some sought political asylum, while others crossed the border to find work, food or medical treatment. Their growing presence in already impoverished South African communities made them particularly vulnerable when violence erupted.

### Government Response Criticized

President **Thabo Mbeki’s** government deployed the military to assist police—the first domestic military deployment since apartheid—but critics said authorities had reacted too slowly and had failed to recognize earlier warnings.

South African leaders condemned the attacks as incompatible with the country’s constitutional commitment to human rights and with the support it had received from other African nations during the anti-apartheid struggle. Yet subsequent outbreaks of anti-immigrant violence have shown that many of the underlying problems—economic inequality, unemployment, poor local governance and hostility toward migrants—remain unresolved.
